prose.hook: This volcanic, mountainous island north of Trinidad and Tobago has no land borders with any country, sitting between the Caribbean Sea and the North Atlantic. Its standout feature is the twin Pitons, Gros Piton and Petit Piton, cone-shaped peaks near Soufrière that rank among the Caribbean's most striking natural sights.
prose.physicalGeography: Saint Lucia is volcanic and mountainous, with broad, fertile valleys cut between the peaks. It lies in the Caribbean Sea, north of Trinidad and Tobago.
prose.climate: The climate is tropical, tempered by northeast trade winds, with a dry season from January to April and a rainy season from May to August; hurricanes occur. The island sits within the volcanic-island arc of the Lesser Antilles, which runs from Saba in the north to Grenada in the south. Mount Gimie, also called Qualibou, is a caldera on the island's west side, while the twin peaks of Gros Piton and Petit Piton are lava-dome remnants tied to the Soufrière volcano; there have been no historical magmatic eruptions, though a minor steam eruption in 1766 scattered a thin layer of ash across a wide area.
prose.economy: Saint Lucia has an upper middle-income, tourism-based economy that is environmentally fragile and dependent on imported energy. It is a major banana producer with a well-educated labor force, and has invested in infrastructure, IT, and communications. Industries include tourism, clothing, assembly of electronic components, beverages, corrugated cardboard boxes, lime processing, and coconut processing, while exports include refined petroleum, gravel and crushed stone, beer, liquor, and paper containers.
prose.peopleAndCulture: English is the official language, alongside Saint Lucian Creole. The population is predominantly of Black or African descent (85.3%), with mixed (10.9%) and East Indian (2.2%) minorities. Religious life is mostly Christian, led by Roman Catholics (61.5%) and Protestants (25.5%, including Seventh Day Adventist, Pentecostal, Baptist, Anglican, and Church of God congregations), with smaller Rastafarian and unaffiliated groups.
